health.bodyAge.body: Two separate estimates, each from a published method: a fitness age from your VO₂ max estimate and a Phenotypic Age from blood results you enter yourself. OpenHoop does not merge them into one number. This is not medical advice.
health.bodyAge.fitness.bandNote: Your VO₂ max estimate ± {see} mL/kg/min, turned into an age. The true value can fall outside this band.
health.bodyAge.fitness.label: Estimated band
health.bodyAge.fitness.meaning: What this means: the age at which healthy Norwegians have, on average, a VO₂ max like your estimate. What it doesn't mean: how old your body is or how healthy you are.
health.bodyAge.fitness.method1: Fitness age is the age at which the average measured VO₂ max of men or women in Loe et al. (PLoS One 2013;8:e64319, Table 2) equals your estimate. A straight line joins the middle of each age group (25, 35 … 75). The 70 and older group counts as 70 to 79.
health.bodyAge.fitness.method2: There are no group averages below 25 or above 75, so then it only says 'younger than' or 'older than'.
health.bodyAge.fitness.method3: The band comes from the typical error of the VO₂ max formula (Uth et al. 2004): ±2.7 mL/kg/min with a measured maximum heart rate, ±4.7 with a predicted one. A few points of VO₂ max quickly add up to ten years.
health.bodyAge.fitness.title: Fitness age
health.bodyAge.fitness.wide: Can't say: the band runs from below {low} to above {high}
health.bodyAge.heading: Body age
health.bodyAge.levelNote: Own estimate following published methods (level C). The two ages are never merged into one. Not a medical age.
health.bodyAge.none.no-sex: Set your sex in your profile
health.bodyAge.none.other-sex: Norms exist for men and women only
health.bodyAge.ownAge: Your age from your birth year: {age}

health.bodyAge.pace.reason.needs-birth-d: Add your full birth date in your profile. The pace compares your age to the day at each blood draw, and a birth year alone can be a year off.
health.bodyAge.pace.reason.needs-two-dra: Needs two complete blood panels at least {days} days apart. Complete panels now: {draws}.
health.bodyAge.pace.reason.too-close: Your complete blood panels are less than {days} days apart. A later panel will give the pace.
health.bodyAge.pace.title: Pace of aging
health.bodyAge.pheno.ageAtDraw: Your age at the blood draw: {age}. It comes from your birth year and can be a year off.
health.bodyAge.pheno.inputs: Blood results: the newest of each, within {window} days
health.bodyAge.pheno.label: From blood tests
health.bodyAge.pheno.meaning: What this means: the age that, on average, goes with your risk of dying according to this model, in a US population study. What it doesn't mean: a diagnosis, or how long you will live.
health.bodyAge.pheno.method1: PhenoAge (Levine et al., Aging 2018;10:573-591): a weighted sum of albumin, creatinine, glucose, ln(CRP in mg/dL), lymphocyte %, MCV, RDW, alkaline phosphatase, white blood cells and age gives a 10-year risk of dying. That is turned into the age with the same average risk.
health.bodyAge.pheno.method2: Formula as corrected in Liu et al. (PLoS Med 2018;15:e1002718, correction 2019), with the unrounded constants from the BioAge package (Kwon and Belsky, GeroScience 2021).
health.bodyAge.pheno.method3: Fitted on about 10,000 US adults (NHANES III) and tested in NHANES IV. For other groups and for a single person it is less certain.
health.bodyAge.pheno.method4: One blood draw varies. CRP can stay higher for days after a cold or hard training, and that pushes the result up. Compare several draws instead.
health.bodyAge.pheno.reason.crp-not-posi: Your CRP is 0. The formula takes the logarithm of CRP, which does not exist for 0, so OpenHoop doesn't calculate. If your report says 'less than' a limit and you enter that limit, the estimate will come out slightly high.
health.bodyAge.pheno.reason.incomplete: Needs all nine blood results below, within {window} days of each other. Missing or too old: {markers}.
health.bodyAge.pheno.reason.invalid-inpu: One of your values can't be right (0, or more than 100 %). Check your results.
health.bodyAge.pheno.reason.no-age: Add your birth year. The formula uses your age at the blood draw.
health.bodyAge.pheno.reason.out-of-range: Your values give a result outside the range of the formula, so no number is shown.
health.bodyAge.pheno.title: Phenotypic Age
health.bodyAge.sourceFitness: From your VO₂ max estimate (fitness age). Add blood results for a Phenotypic Age.
health.bodyAge.sourcePheno: From your blood tests (Phenotypic Age). The fitness age below stays separate.

health.contrib.basis.ageSex: Typical range for your age and sex
health.contrib.leanMass.advice: Strength training and enough protein help keep lean mass, which tends to drop with age. Weigh at the same time of day for a fair trend.
health.contrib.leanMass.source: Weight × (1 − body fat %) from your latest entry that has a body fat value. There is no published target by age.
health.contrib.moderateVigorous.advice: Brisk walks, easy cycling and swimming count. Spread the minutes over the week, for example 30 minutes on five days.
health.contrib.moderateVigorous.source: Minutes in heart rate zones 1 to 5. With automatic zones, zone 1 starts at 40 % of your heart rate reserve, where moderate intensity begins (Garber et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011). Target: WHO 2020, 150–300 minutes of moderate-or-vigorous activity a week; vigorous minutes count at least as much (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451-1462).
health.contrib.moderateVigorous.sourceCu: Minutes in heart rate zones 1 to 5, with the zone limits you set yourself, so zone 1 may not start exactly where moderate intensity begins. Target: WHO 2020, 150–300 minutes of moderate-or-vigorous activity a week (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451-1462).
health.contrib.reason.needs-baseline: Needs 3 of the last 7 nights and 4 nights before them
health.contrib.reason.needs-days: Needs at least 4 worn days in the last 4 weeks
health.contrib.reason.needs-nights: Needs at least 4 nights in the last 4 weeks
health.contrib.reason.no-body-fat: Enter a body fat % to work it out
health.contrib.reason.no-sessions: No strength sessions logged in the last 4 weeks
health.contrib.restingHr.advice: Resting heart rate drops with regular endurance training, enough sleep and less alcohol. A sudden rise can point to illness or poor recovery.
health.contrib.restingHr.source: Compared with your own usual range over the 30 nights before last week, not with a population target. A sleeping resting heart rate is lower than an awake one.
health.contrib.sleepConsistency.advice: Go to bed and get up within the same half hour every day, weekends too. A fixed wake time does most of the work.
health.contrib.sleepConsistency.source: OpenHoop's own consistency score (level C): how much your bed and wake times shift from night to night. No guideline sets a target for it.
health.contrib.sleepHours.advice: Plan bedtime back from your wake time: your sleep need plus about 20 minutes to fall asleep. Keep the last hour before bed calm and dim.
health.contrib.sleepHours.source: Target from the US National Sleep Foundation: 7–9 hours for adults up to 64, 7–8 hours from 65 (Hirshkowitz et al., Sleep Health 2015;1:40-43).
health.contrib.steps.advice: Add a short walk after meals or take the stairs. Short walks add up over the day.
health.contrib.steps.source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 2022;7:e219-e228: across 15 studies the lower risk of death levelled off at about 6,000–8,000 steps a day from age 60 and 8,000–10,000 below 60.
health.contrib.strength.advice: Two sessions a week that work all major muscle groups meet the WHO advice. Body-weight exercises count.
health.contrib.strength.source: WHO 2020: muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days a week. Counted from the strength sessions you log in OpenHoop.
health.contrib.strengthMinutes: About {value} minutes of strength training a week
health.contrib.target.age-out-of-range: No reference values for your age
health.contrib.target.no-age: Add your birth year to see the target for your age
health.contrib.target.no-sex: Set your sex to compare with people your age
health.contrib.target.none-published: No published target: follow your own trend
health.contrib.target.other-sex: Reference values exist for men and women only
health.contrib.vo2max.advice: Regular endurance training with some harder intervals raises VO₂ max over weeks to months. The estimate follows your resting heart rate.
health.contrib.vo2max.source: The middle range (average ± 1 standard deviation) of treadmill tests in healthy Norwegians of your age and sex (Loe et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e64319). Yours is an estimate.
health.contrib.zones45.advice: Short hard efforts add these minutes, for example 6 × 1 minute hard with 2 minutes easy in between, once or twice a week. Build up slowly.
health.contrib.zones45.source: Zones 4 and 5 start at 80 % of your heart rate reserve. No guideline sets a target for these zones alone; the WHO counts every vigorous minute, from 60 % of your reserve, towards 75–150 minutes a week.
health.contrib.zones45.sourceCustom: Zones 4 and 5 with the zone limits you set yourself. No guideline sets a target for these zones alone; the WHO counts every vigorous minute towards 75–150 minutes a week.

health.mg.disclaimer: OpenHoop is not a medical device. It never shows a rhythm verdict or a blood pressure value.
health.mg.needsBody: This feature needs the sensors of the MG band. Your band does not have them, so nothing can be measured here.
health.notOffered.title: Not part of OpenHoop
health.pillar.activity.days: Measured on {days} of 7 days, {full} of them for 10 hours or more
health.pillar.activity.empty: No heart rate minutes measured in the last 7 days.
health.pillar.activity.inputs: Minutes of heart rate from the band, your resting heart rate and your maximum heart rate.
health.pillar.activity.method: A minute counts when its heart rate reaches 40 % of your heart rate reserve, the lower bound of moderate intensity (Garber et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43:1334-1359). Every such minute counts once. The WHO counts a vigorous minute as two (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451-1462), so this count is on the low side. Heart rate is only a stand-in for intensity: heat, stress and caffeine raise it too.
health.pillar.activity.reference: WHO: 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity
health.pillar.activity.status.above-rang: More than 300 minutes. According to the WHO, more activity brings further benefit.
health.pillar.activity.status.below: Below the 150 minutes the WHO recommends for adults.
health.pillar.activity.status.in-range: Within the range the WHO recommends for adults.
health.pillar.activity.status.incomplete: Below 150 minutes so far, but the band did not measure all 7 days for 10 hours or more, so OpenHoop does not judge this week.
health.pillar.body: Four areas that matter for long-term health, each from what the band measured and compared with a published reference or with your own history. There is no combined score.
health.pillar.fitness.inputs: Your VO₂ max estimate, sex and age.
health.pillar.fitness.method: Your VO₂ max estimate compared with treadmill reference values for your sex and age group (Loe et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e64319).
health.pillar.heading: Healthspan pillars
health.pillar.recovery.inputs: Nightly HRV and resting heart rate measured by the band.
health.pillar.recovery.method: The average of the last 7 nights is compared with your own range (average ± 1 standard deviation) over the 30 nights before them. Higher or lower is not good or bad by itself: illness, alcohol, training and stress all move these values.
health.pillar.recovery.missing: Needs at least 3 of the last 7 nights and 4 nights in the 30 before them.
health.pillar.sleep.empty: Needs at least {min} nights of sleep in the last 7 days.
health.pillar.sleep.inputs: Sleep duration, sleep need and sleep consistency from {nights} of the last 7 nights.
health.pillar.sleep.met: On average you slept 7 hours or more, the amount recommended for adults.
health.pillar.sleep.method: Averages over the last 7 nights. Duration is compared with the recommendation of at least 7 hours a night for adults (Watson et al., Sleep 2015;38:843-844) and with OpenHoop's own sleep need. Regularity is OpenHoop's sleep consistency.
health.pillar.sleep.notMet: On average you slept less than the 7 hours recommended for adults.
health.pillar.title: Healthspan pillars
health.pregnancy.baseline.body: Resting heart rate often rises during pregnancy. These tiles compare you with your own last 30 nights, so a slow rise does not count as unusual. Readiness itself is not changed.
health.pregnancy.baseline.title: Adjusted baselines
health.pregnancy.body: Enter your due date to count weeks and follow your nightly numbers as trends. This is not medical advice.
health.pregnancy.disclaimer: OpenHoop does not give medical advice. Ask your midwife or doctor about anything you notice.
health.pregnancy.field.dueHint: YYYY-MM-DD, from 2 weeks ago up to 40 weeks ahead
health.pregnancy.heading: Pregnancy mode

health.pregnancy.privacy: Stored only on this phone and included in your export. Turning pregnancy mode off deletes the due date.
health.pregnancy.title: Pregnancy

health.pregnancy.week.before: The due date you entered puts the start of the pregnancy in the future, so no week is shown.

health.symptoms.body: Note how you feel so you can look back for patterns. OpenHoop only shows what you logged and does not interpret it.
health.symptoms.error.day: Enter the day as YYYY-MM-DD, today or earlier.
health.symptoms.error.flowInside: This day is in the middle of a logged period. Change that period on the Cycle screen.
health.symptoms.error.flowInvalid: That flow would make a period that overlaps another one or runs too long. Check your log on the Cycle screen.
health.symptoms.error.symptom: Pick a symptom or set the flow.
health.symptoms.flowHint: Logs this day in your period log on the Cycle screen. A day up to 2 days after or before a logged period joins that period. Flow is kept per period, so it applies to the whole period.
health.symptoms.flowPeriod: This day is part of your period from {from} to {to}. Changing the flow changes it for that whole period.

health.symptoms.newPeriod: {day} is not next to a logged period, so this starts a new period. Start it?

health.vitals.empty: No vitals yet. They appear after the first night with the band.
health.vitals.footnote: Your range is the average of the previous 30 days plus or minus one standard deviation. It is not a medical reference range.

health.vitals.lastSync: Last sync {ago} · pull down to sync
health.vitals.levelNote: Measured by the band while you sleep: blood oxygen and skin temperature are level A, the other three level B. Tap a tile for its 30-day trend and your personal range.

health.vitals.notSynced: Not synced yet · pull down to sync
health.vitals.title: Vitals
health.vo2max.body: An estimate of your aerobic fitness from your resting and maximum heart rate. It comes from a population formula, not from a measurement, and can be several points off for you.
health.vo2max.error: Typical error in the original study: ±{see} mL/kg/min. For you it can be larger.
health.vo2max.heading: VO₂ max estimate
health.vo2max.inputs.restingHint: Median of {nights} nights in the last {window} days
health.vo2max.inputs.title: Inputs
health.vo2max.level.method: The five levels split that group into fifths, worked out from its published average and standard deviation as if the values follow a bell curve. The level names are OpenHoop's.
health.vo2max.level.title: Fitness level
health.vo2max.levelNote: Estimated from your resting and maximum heart rate (level C). The method and its limits are below.
health.vo2max.method.formula: VO₂ max ≈ 15.3 × maximum heart rate ÷ resting heart rate (Uth et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2004;91:111-115). Without a maximum in your profile: 208 − 0.7 × age (Tanaka et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2001;37:153-156).
health.vo2max.method.limit1: The formula was fitted on 46 well-trained men aged 21 to 51. The authors say other groups, such as women and untrained people, still need to be checked.
health.vo2max.method.limit2: In that study the typical error was 2.7 mL/kg/min with a measured maximum heart rate and 4.7 with one predicted from age.
health.vo2max.method.limit3: OpenHoop's resting heart rate is the lowest 5-minute average during sleep. That is usually lower than a resting heart rate taken awake, so this estimate may read high.
health.vo2max.method.limit4: A maximum heart rate from a real all-out effort, entered in your profile, gives a better estimate than one predicted from age.
health.vo2max.method.title: Method and limits
health.vo2max.norm.above: Your estimate is more than one standard deviation above that group's average.
health.vo2max.norm.below: Your estimate is more than one standard deviation below that group's average.
health.vo2max.norm.reason.age-out-of-ran: The reference values start at age 20, so no comparison is shown.
health.vo2max.norm.reason.no-age: Add your birth year to compare with people your age.
health.vo2max.norm.reason.no-sex: Set your sex in your profile to compare with reference values. They are published per sex.
health.vo2max.norm.reason.other-sex: The reference values are published for men and women only, so no comparison is shown.
health.vo2max.norm.source: Reference: treadmill measurements in healthy Norwegian adults (Loe et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e64319). Theirs were measured and yours is estimated, so treat the comparison as rough.
health.vo2max.norm.title: Compared with people your age
health.vo2max.norm.within: Your estimate is within one standard deviation of that group's average.
health.vo2max.reason.no-max-hr: Needs your birth year or your maximum heart rate. Add one in your profile.
health.vo2max.reason.no-resting-hr: Needs a resting heart rate from at least {min} nights in the last {window} days. Now: {nights}.
health.vo2max.reason.out-of-range: Your inputs give a value outside a plausible range, so no estimate is shown. Check your maximum heart rate in your profile.
health.vo2max.short.no-max-hr: Needs birth year or max HR
health.vo2max.title: VO₂ max

health.vo2max.trend.hint: Last {days} days. Each day uses the {window} nights up to it.
health.vo2max.trend.title: Trend

journal.voice.blocked: The microphone is switched off for OpenHoop. Allow it in the phone's settings to dictate, or type the note.
journal.voice.denied: Dictation needs the microphone. Tap Dictate again to allow it, or type the note.
journal.voice.downloadFailed: The language pack could not be downloaded. Check your connection and try again.
journal.voice.downloadStarted: The download started. Android finishes it in the background and may wait for Wi-Fi. Tap Check again when it is done.
journal.voice.failed: Dictation stopped because the speech recogniser reported an error. Try again, or type the note.
journal.voice.languageMissing: The on-device speech recogniser has no offline language pack for {language}, so dictation is off. Typing works everywhere.
journal.voice.languagePack: The offline language pack for {language} is not installed on this phone. Android downloads it through its own speech service, not through OpenHoop, and it needs a connection once.
journal.voice.listening: Listening. Speak now and tap Stop when you are done. The text lands in the note above, where you can correct it before you save.
journal.voice.onDevice: Dictation runs on this phone only. The audio is not saved and not sent anywhere. Nothing is saved until you tap Save note.
journal.voice.unavailableAndroid: Dictation needs Android 13 or later, because only then can the phone's own speech recogniser be required to work offline. Typing works everywhere.
journal.voice.unavailableIos: Dictation is not available on iPhone yet. iOS can fall back to Apple's servers when a language has no model on the phone, and OpenHoop never allows that. Typing works everywhere.
journal.voice.unavailableRecogniser: This phone has no on-device speech recogniser, or it is not available right now, so dictation is off. OpenHoop never sends audio to an online service. Typing works everywhere.
loadTarget.hidden.body: Load targets are hidden while pregnancy mode is on. Your Load is still shown, without a target. Turn targets back on in Pregnancy.
loadTarget.hidden.buzz: Paused: Load targets are hidden in pregnancy mode.
loadTarget.hidden.pill: Load targets hidden in pregnancy mode
network.labs.sends: Sends: only the PDF or photo of a lab report that you choose to read with Claude, at the moment you start it, with your own API key. None of your other data is sent.
network.labs.title: Read lab reports with Claude
network.labs.to: To: Anthropic (api.anthropic.com), under Anthropic's privacy policy and the data retention of your own API account. Reading a report on your phone never uses the network.
stress.calibratingBody: Stress compares you with your own normal. It needs {needed} days with at least an hour of still, awake time first.
stress.disclaimer: OpenHoop's own estimate (level C), not a diagnosis. It is not a medical device and cannot tell stress from caffeine, illness, heat or alcohol, which also raise heart rate.
stress.methodBody: Every 5 minutes of still, awake time outside workouts and the 30 minutes after them is compared with your own baseline of up to 14 earlier days. A higher heart rate and a lower HRV (RMSSD) raise the score. 0 means at or below your normal and each point is one standard deviation above it, up to 3. Low is below 1, medium from 1, high from 2.
stress.noWindows: No still, awake moments to score on this day
term.bodyAge.body: Body age puts a number on how your body compares with others: a fitness age from your VO₂ max estimate, or a Phenotypic Age from nine blood results you enter. Below your real age is a good sign. The two ages are kept apart.
term.bodyAge.full: An age from your fitness or blood tests
term.bodyAge.line: An age worked out from your VO₂ max or your blood results, next to your real age.
term.bodyAge.method: Fitness age follows the Loe 2013 reference values; Phenotypic Age follows Levine 2018. OpenHoop's own estimate, not a medical age.
term.vo2max.body: VO₂ max is the most oxygen your body can use per kilogram per minute at full effort. Higher means fitter. OpenHoop estimates it from your resting and maximum heart rate; a lab test measures it.
term.vo2max.line: How much oxygen your body can use at full effort, estimated from your heart rate.
term.vo2max.method: Uth et al. 2004 formula from resting and maximum heart rate. The typical error is several mL/kg/min.
